items.title: I can classify a reaction as a substitution reaction given an equation or description
items.what: A substitution reaction is one where an atom or group of atoms in a molecule is replaced by a different atom or group of atoms, leaving the carbon skeleton intact.
items.why: Correctly identifying reaction type is the first step in predicting products and writing equations. Misclassifying a reaction leads to incorrect products and lost marks.
items.example: In the reaction CH3CH2Br + NaOH(aq) → CH3CH2OH + NaBr, the Br is replaced by OH, making this a substitution reaction.

subtopic.name: Substitution Reactions
subtopic.what: Substitution reactions involve replacing one atom or group of atoms in a molecule with another. This section covers two main types: halogenation of alkanes under UV light, and reactions of haloalkanes with hydroxide ions or ammonia.
subtopic.why: Substitution reactions are a foundational tool in organic synthesis, allowing chemists to introduce new functional groups such as halogens, hydroxyl groups and amino groups into carbon chains. Understanding these reactions is essential for designing multi-step synthesis pathways.

items.title: I can write the equation for the halogenation of an alkane under UV light to form a haloalkane
items.what: Alkanes react with Cl2 or Br2 in the presence of UV light. A halogen atom replaces one hydrogen atom on the alkane, producing a haloalkane and a hydrogen halide (HCl or HBr) as a by-product.
items.why: This is one of the primary methods to introduce a halogen functional group onto a saturated carbon chain, which can then be used as an intermediate in further synthesis steps.
items.example: CH3CH3 + Br2 → CH3CH2Br + HBr (UV light). Ethane reacts with bromine under UV light to give bromoethane and hydrogen bromide.

subtopic.name: Substitution Reactions
subtopic.what: Substitution reactions involve replacing one atom or group of atoms in a molecule with another. This section covers two main types: halogenation of alkanes under UV light, and reactions of haloalkanes with hydroxide ions or ammonia.
subtopic.why: Substitution reactions are a foundational tool in organic synthesis, allowing chemists to introduce new functional groups such as halogens, hydroxyl groups and amino groups into carbon chains. Understanding these reactions is essential for designing multi-step synthesis pathways.

items.title: I can explain why halogenation of larger alkanes can produce a mixture of positional isomers
items.what: When an alkane has more than one type of hydrogen (e.g. on different carbons), the halogen can substitute at any of those positions, leading to a mixture of structurally different haloalkane products.
items.why: Understanding this limitation is important when designing efficient synthesis pathways. A mixture of products reduces the yield of the desired compound and complicates purification.
items.example: Propane reacting with Cl2 under UV light gives both 1-chloropropane (Cl on carbon 1) and 2-chloropropane (Cl on carbon 2) simultaneously.

subtopic.what: Substitution reactions involve replacing one atom or group of atoms in a molecule with another. This section covers two main types: halogenation of alkanes under UV light, and reactions of haloalkanes with hydroxide ions or ammonia.
subtopic.why: Substitution reactions are a foundational tool in organic synthesis, allowing chemists to introduce new functional groups such as halogens, hydroxyl groups and amino groups into carbon chains. Understanding these reactions is essential for designing multi-step synthesis pathways.

items.title: I can write the equation for the reaction of a haloalkane with aqueous NaOH or KOH to form a primary alcohol
items.what: Haloalkanes react with aqueous metal hydroxides such as NaOH(aq) or KOH(aq). The hydroxide ion (OH−) replaces the halogen atom, producing an alcohol and a metal halide salt as a by-product.
items.why: This reaction is a key step in multi-step pathways for synthesising primary alcohols and ultimately carboxylic acids from alkane or alkene starting materials.
items.example: CH3CH2CH2Cl + NaOH(aq) → CH3CH2CH2OH + NaCl. 1-chloropropane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give propan-1-ol and sodium chloride.

subtopic.what: Substitution reactions involve replacing one atom or group of atoms in a molecule with another. This section covers two main types: halogenation of alkanes under UV light, and reactions of haloalkanes with hydroxide ions or ammonia.
subtopic.why: Substitution reactions are a foundational tool in organic synthesis, allowing chemists to introduce new functional groups such as halogens, hydroxyl groups and amino groups into carbon chains. Understanding these reactions is essential for designing multi-step synthesis pathways.

items.title: I can write the equation for the reaction of a haloalkane with ammonia to form a primary amine
items.what: Haloalkanes react with ammonia (NH3). The NH2 group from ammonia replaces the halogen atom, installing an amino group on the carbon chain. The by-product is a hydrogen halide such as HCl, HBr or HI.
items.why: This substitution reaction is one of only two pathways in the study design for synthesising primary amines, making it an essential reaction to know for multi-step synthesis questions.
items.example: CH3CH2Br + NH3 → CH3CH2NH2 + HBr. Bromoethane reacts with ammonia to give ethanamine and hydrogen bromide.

subtopic.why: Substitution reactions are a foundational tool in organic synthesis, allowing chemists to introduce new functional groups such as halogens, hydroxyl groups and amino groups into carbon chains. Understanding these reactions is essential for designing multi-step synthesis pathways.

items.title: I can classify a reaction as an addition reaction given an equation or description
items.what: An addition reaction requires an unsaturated reactant (containing a C=C double bond). Two reactants combine to form a single larger product with no atoms lost as by-products.
items.why: Identifying addition reactions correctly allows you to predict that the product will be saturated and that no by-product will form, which affects atom economy calculations.
items.example: CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3CH3. Ethene and hydrogen combine to form ethane with no by-product, making this an addition reaction.

subtopic.name: Addition Reactions of Alkenes
subtopic.what: Addition reactions involve adding a small molecule across the carbon-carbon double bond of an alkene. The double bond breaks and each carbon forms a new single bond with part of the added molecule, producing a saturated product.
subtopic.why: Alkenes are versatile starting materials because different addition reactions install different functional groups, making them central to organic synthesis of alcohols, haloalkanes and alkanes.

items.title: I can write the equation for the hydrogenation of an alkene using H2 and a metal catalyst
items.what: Hydrogenation adds H2 across the C=C double bond of an alkene in the presence of a transition metal catalyst such as Ni, Pd or Pt. The product is a fully saturated alkane.
items.why: Hydrogenation is used industrially to produce fuels and food products such as margarine. It is also a 100% atom economy reaction since the H2 is fully incorporated into the product.
items.example: CH3CH=CHCH3 + H2 → CH3CH2CH2CH3 (Pd catalyst). But-2-ene reacts with hydrogen over palladium to give butane.

subtopic.name: Addition Reactions of Alkenes
subtopic.what: Addition reactions involve adding a small molecule across the carbon-carbon double bond of an alkene. The double bond breaks and each carbon forms a new single bond with part of the added molecule, producing a saturated product.
subtopic.why: Alkenes are versatile starting materials because different addition reactions install different functional groups, making them central to organic synthesis of alcohols, haloalkanes and alkanes.

items.title: I can write the equation for the halogenation of an alkene using Cl2 or Br2
items.what: Halogenation adds Cl2 or Br2 across the C=C double bond. Both halogen atoms are added, one to each carbon of the double bond, giving a dihaloalkane product.
items.why: Halogenation of alkenes is used in the synthesis of solvents, refrigerants and pharmaceutical precursors. It is also a 100% atom economy addition reaction.
items.example: CH2=CH2 + Br2 → CH2BrCH2Br. Ethene reacts with bromine to give 1,2-dibromoethane.

subtopic.name: Addition Reactions of Alkenes
subtopic.what: Addition reactions involve adding a small molecule across the carbon-carbon double bond of an alkene. The double bond breaks and each carbon forms a new single bond with part of the added molecule, producing a saturated product.
subtopic.why: Alkenes are versatile starting materials because different addition reactions install different functional groups, making them central to organic synthesis of alcohols, haloalkanes and alkanes.

items.title: I can write the equation for the hydrohalogenation of an alkene using HCl, HBr or HI
items.what: Hydrohalogenation adds a hydrogen halide (HX) across the C=C double bond. The H adds to one carbon and the X adds to the other, giving a haloalkane product.
items.why: This reaction is important for synthesising haloalkane intermediates from alkene starting materials as part of Pathway 2 for making amines and carboxylic acids.
items.example: CH3CH=CH2 + HBr → CH3CHBrCH3 + CH3CH2CH2Br. Propene reacts with HBr to give a mixture of 2-bromopropane and 1-bromopropane.

subtopic.name: Addition Reactions of Alkenes
subtopic.what: Addition reactions involve adding a small molecule across the carbon-carbon double bond of an alkene. The double bond breaks and each carbon forms a new single bond with part of the added molecule, producing a saturated product.
subtopic.why: Alkenes are versatile starting materials because different addition reactions install different functional groups, making them central to organic synthesis of alcohols, haloalkanes and alkanes.

items.title: I can explain why hydrohalogenation of an unsymmetric alkene produces two positional isomers
items.what: When the alkene is not symmetric (the two carbons of the double bond are not equivalent), the HX molecule can add in two orientations. This produces two different haloalkane positional isomers as a mixture.
items.why: Knowing which product is the major or desired product is important for pathway design. Choosing a symmetric alkene where possible avoids this problem and improves yield of the target compound.
items.example: Propene (CH3CH=CH2) reacting with HCl gives both 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane because the two carbons of the double bond are not equivalent.

subtopic.name: Addition Reactions of Alkenes
subtopic.what: Addition reactions involve adding a small molecule across the carbon-carbon double bond of an alkene. The double bond breaks and each carbon forms a new single bond with part of the added molecule, producing a saturated product.
subtopic.why: Alkenes are versatile starting materials because different addition reactions install different functional groups, making them central to organic synthesis of alcohols, haloalkanes and alkanes.

items.title: I can write the equation for the hydration of an alkene using H2O with an acid catalyst at high temperature
items.what: Hydration adds water (H2O) across the C=C double bond in the presence of a catalyst such as H3PO4 or H2SO4 at temperatures of 150–200°C. The product is an alcohol.
items.why: Hydration of alkenes is an important industrial route for producing alcohols such as ethanol, which serves as a solvent, fuel and chemical feedstock.
items.example: CH2=CH2 + H2O → CH3CH2OH (H3PO4, 150°C). Ethene reacts with water over phosphoric acid to give ethanol.

subtopic.name: Addition Reactions of Alkenes
subtopic.what: Addition reactions involve adding a small molecule across the carbon-carbon double bond of an alkene. The double bond breaks and each carbon forms a new single bond with part of the added molecule, producing a saturated product.
subtopic.why: Alkenes are versatile starting materials because different addition reactions install different functional groups, making them central to organic synthesis of alcohols, haloalkanes and alkanes.

items.title: I can identify the best alkene starting material to produce a specific alcohol from a hydration reaction
items.what: When more than one alkene could give the desired alcohol, a symmetric alkene is preferred because it produces only one product. An unsymmetric alkene would give a mixture of two alcohols, reducing the yield of the target compound.
items.why: Selecting the optimal starting material is a key skill in reaction pathway design. It connects to atom economy and overall yield, which are assessed in 9C.
items.example: To make hexan-3-ol, hex-3-ene is preferred over hex-2-ene. Hex-3-ene is symmetric and gives only hexan-3-ol, while hex-2-ene gives a mixture of hexan-3-ol and hexan-2-ol.

subtopic.why: Alkenes are versatile starting materials because different addition reactions install different functional groups, making them central to organic synthesis of alcohols, haloalkanes and alkanes.

items.title: I can classify a reaction as an oxidation reaction given an equation or description
items.what: An oxidation reaction in organic chemistry involves the loss of electrons, which is typically seen as the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen at a functional group. A primary alcohol oxidised to a carboxylic acid is the main example in this topic.
items.why: Recognising oxidation reactions is necessary to identify which step in a pathway converts an alcohol intermediate into the target carboxylic acid product.
items.example: CH3CH2OH → CH3COOH using acidified KMnO4. The alcohol gains an oxygen and loses two hydrogens, representing an oxidation.

subtopic.name: Oxidation and Reaction Pathways
subtopic.what: Primary alcohols can be oxidised to carboxylic acids (or aldehydes) using acidified oxidising agents such as KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7. This reaction, combined with substitution and addition reactions, enables multi-step synthesis pathways to amines and carboxylic acids.
subtopic.why: Reaction pathways allow chemists to build complex target molecules from simple, inexpensive starting materials over multiple steps. Mastering pathway design is a central skill in VCE Chemistry Unit 4.

items.title: I can write the equation for the oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid using acidified KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7
items.what: Primary alcohols react with acidified potassium permanganate (H+/KMnO4 or H+/MnO4−) or acidified potassium dichromate (H+/K2Cr2O7 or H+/Cr2O72−) with heat to give a carboxylic acid. Water is also produced.
items.why: This is the final step in the two main carboxylic acid synthesis pathways and is a common step in multi-step exam questions. Knowing both oxidising agents and the condition of heat is required.
items.example: CH3CH2CH2OH + H+/Cr2O72− → CH3CH2COOH + H2O (heat). Propan-1-ol is oxidised to propanoic acid using acidified potassium dichromate.

subtopic.name: Oxidation and Reaction Pathways
subtopic.what: Primary alcohols can be oxidised to carboxylic acids (or aldehydes) using acidified oxidising agents such as KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7. This reaction, combined with substitution and addition reactions, enables multi-step synthesis pathways to amines and carboxylic acids.
subtopic.why: Reaction pathways allow chemists to build complex target molecules from simple, inexpensive starting materials over multiple steps. Mastering pathway design is a central skill in VCE Chemistry Unit 4.

items.title: I can draw a two-step or three-step reaction pathway to synthesise a primary amine from an alkane or alkene
items.what: Pathway from alkane: (1) halogenation with Cl2 or Br2 under UV light gives haloalkane, (2) reaction with NH3 gives primary amine. Pathway from alkene: (1) hydrohalogenation with HCl, HBr or HI gives haloalkane, (2) reaction with NH3 gives primary amine.
items.why: These are the two prescribed pathways for amine synthesis in the Study Design. Being able to draw the full pathway including reagents, conditions and intermediate structures is a high-value exam skill.
items.example: To synthesise ethanamine from ethene: Step 1 — CH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3CH2Br. Step 2 — CH3CH2Br + NH3 → CH3CH2NH2 + HBr.

subtopic.name: Oxidation and Reaction Pathways
subtopic.what: Primary alcohols can be oxidised to carboxylic acids (or aldehydes) using acidified oxidising agents such as KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7. This reaction, combined with substitution and addition reactions, enables multi-step synthesis pathways to amines and carboxylic acids.
subtopic.why: Reaction pathways allow chemists to build complex target molecules from simple, inexpensive starting materials over multiple steps. Mastering pathway design is a central skill in VCE Chemistry Unit 4.

items.title: I can draw a two-step or three-step reaction pathway to synthesise a carboxylic acid from an alkane or alkene
items.what: Pathway from alkane: (1) halogenation under UV light, (2) substitution with NaOH(aq) to give alcohol, (3) oxidation with H+/KMnO4 or H+/K2Cr2O7 to give carboxylic acid. Pathway from alkene: (1) hydration gives alcohol directly, (2) oxidation gives carboxylic acid.
items.why: These are the two prescribed pathways for carboxylic acid synthesis. The alkene pathway is more efficient (fewer steps) and connects to atom economy discussions in 9C.
items.example: To synthesise ethanoic acid from ethene: Step 1 — CH2=CH2 + H2O → CH3CH2OH (H3PO4, 300°C). Step 2 — CH3CH2OH → CH3COOH (H+/Cr2O72−, heat).

subtopic.what: Primary alcohols can be oxidised to carboxylic acids (or aldehydes) using acidified oxidising agents such as KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7. This reaction, combined with substitution and addition reactions, enables multi-step synthesis pathways to amines and carboxylic acids.
subtopic.why: Reaction pathways allow chemists to build complex target molecules from simple, inexpensive starting materials over multiple steps. Mastering pathway design is a central skill in VCE Chemistry Unit 4.

items.title: I can identify and justify the factors that make a reaction pathway efficient and sustainable
items.what: Key factors in pathway design include: fewest steps possible, mild reaction conditions, cheap and readily available starting materials, stable intermediates, low-toxicity reagents and by-products, and a high overall yield.
items.why: Exam questions often ask students to compare or justify pathway choices. Understanding these factors links reaction pathways to the green chemistry and sustainability content in 9C.
items.example: A two-step pathway from ethene to ethanoic acid is preferred over a three-step pathway from ethane because it requires fewer reagents, fewer steps, and uses the more reactive alkene starting material.

subtopic.what: Primary alcohols can be oxidised to carboxylic acids (or aldehydes) using acidified oxidising agents such as KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7. This reaction, combined with substitution and addition reactions, enables multi-step synthesis pathways to amines and carboxylic acids.
subtopic.why: Reaction pathways allow chemists to build complex target molecules from simple, inexpensive starting materials over multiple steps. Mastering pathway design is a central skill in VCE Chemistry Unit 4.

items.title: I can classify a reaction as condensation or hydrolysis given an equation or description
items.what: Condensation reactions produce a larger molecule and release a small molecule such as water. Hydrolysis reactions use water to break a bond and produce two smaller molecules. They are the reverse of each other.
items.why: Correctly classifying these reactions is necessary before writing equations or identifying products. Condensation and hydrolysis appear in both ester chemistry and biological molecule contexts.
items.example: Glycerol + 3 fatty acids → triglyceride + 3H2O is condensation. Triglyceride + 3H2O → glycerol + 3 fatty acids is hydrolysis.

subtopic.name: Condensation and Hydrolysis Reactions
subtopic.what: Condensation reactions join two molecules together with the release of a small molecule (usually water), forming esters, peptides, glycosidic bonds and triglycerides. Hydrolysis is the reverse process, using water to break large molecules into smaller components.
subtopic.why: These reactions underpin the formation and digestion of the major biological macromolecules — lipids, proteins and carbohydrates — and are essential for understanding both biochemistry and industrial organic chemistry.

items.title: I can write the equation for the esterification reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol
items.what: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol react in the presence of a concentrated acid catalyst (H2SO4) and heat to form an ester and water. The ester linkage (−COO−) is formed when the −OH of the acid and the −H of the alcohol combine to leave as water.
items.why: Esterification is a high-frequency exam reaction. Students must be able to draw structural formulas of both reactants and products and identify the correct catalyst and conditions.
items.example: CH3COOH + CH3CH2OH → CH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O (H2SO4, heat). Ethanoic acid and ethanol react to give ethyl ethanoate and water.

subtopic.name: Condensation and Hydrolysis Reactions
subtopic.what: Condensation reactions join two molecules together with the release of a small molecule (usually water), forming esters, peptides, glycosidic bonds and triglycerides. Hydrolysis is the reverse process, using water to break large molecules into smaller components.
subtopic.why: These reactions underpin the formation and digestion of the major biological macromolecules — lipids, proteins and carbohydrates — and are essential for understanding both biochemistry and industrial organic chemistry.

items.title: I can write the equation for the hydrolysis of an ester under basic conditions
items.what: Esters are hydrolysed using water in the presence of a base such as NaOH or KOH. This saponification reaction breaks the ester linkage to produce a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Excess water drives the reaction to completion.
items.why: Ester hydrolysis is the reverse of esterification and is important for understanding how soaps are made and how fats are digested. It is a direct application of the Study Design requirement for hydrolysis equations.
items.example: CH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O → CH3COOH + CH3CH2OH (NaOH catalyst). Ethyl ethanoate is hydrolysed to ethanoic acid and ethanol.

subtopic.name: Condensation and Hydrolysis Reactions
subtopic.what: Condensation reactions join two molecules together with the release of a small molecule (usually water), forming esters, peptides, glycosidic bonds and triglycerides. Hydrolysis is the reverse process, using water to break large molecules into smaller components.
subtopic.why: These reactions underpin the formation and digestion of the major biological macromolecules — lipids, proteins and carbohydrates — and are essential for understanding both biochemistry and industrial organic chemistry.

items.title: I can write the equation for the condensation reaction that forms a triglyceride from glycerol and fatty acids
items.what: Three fatty acid molecules react with one glycerol molecule in three condensation reactions catalysed by enzymes. Three ester bonds are formed and three water molecules are released as by-products.
items.why: Triglycerides are the main form of fat storage in living organisms and are the starting material for biodiesel production. Understanding their formation is foundational for both biological and industrial chemistry.
items.example: C3H8O3 (glycerol) + 3 C17H35COOH (stearic acid) → triglyceride + 3H2O (enzyme catalyst).

subtopic.name: Condensation and Hydrolysis Reactions
subtopic.what: Condensation reactions join two molecules together with the release of a small molecule (usually water), forming esters, peptides, glycosidic bonds and triglycerides. Hydrolysis is the reverse process, using water to break large molecules into smaller components.
subtopic.why: These reactions underpin the formation and digestion of the major biological macromolecules — lipids, proteins and carbohydrates — and are essential for understanding both biochemistry and industrial organic chemistry.

items.title: I can write the equation for the hydrolysis of a triglyceride to give glycerol and fatty acids
items.what: Triglycerides are hydrolysed in the presence of enzymes (e.g. lipase in the digestive system) or NaOH to give one glycerol molecule and three fatty acid molecules. Three water molecules are consumed.
items.why: This reaction explains how our bodies break down dietary fats for energy and is also the basis of saponification, the industrial production of soap.
items.example: Triglyceride + 3H2O → C3H8O3 (glycerol) + 3 fatty acids (lipase or NaOH). The three ester bonds in the triglyceride are each broken by one water molecule.

subtopic.name: Condensation and Hydrolysis Reactions
subtopic.what: Condensation reactions join two molecules together with the release of a small molecule (usually water), forming esters, peptides, glycosidic bonds and triglycerides. Hydrolysis is the reverse process, using water to break large molecules into smaller components.
subtopic.why: These reactions underpin the formation and digestion of the major biological macromolecules — lipids, proteins and carbohydrates — and are essential for understanding both biochemistry and industrial organic chemistry.

items.title: I can write the equation for the condensation reaction that forms a dipeptide or tripeptide from amino acids
items.what: The carboxyl group (−COOH) of one 2-amino acid reacts with the amino group (−NH2) of another in a condensation reaction. A peptide bond (amide bond, −CO−NH−) forms and one water molecule is released per bond formed.
items.why: Proteins are essential biological molecules. Understanding how peptide bonds form and break links organic chemistry to biochemistry and is directly tested in exam questions involving amino acid structures.
items.example: Alanine + tyrosine → alanyl-tyrosine dipeptide + H2O (ribosome/enzyme). One peptide bond forms and one water molecule is released.

subtopic.name: Condensation and Hydrolysis Reactions
subtopic.what: Condensation reactions join two molecules together with the release of a small molecule (usually water), forming esters, peptides, glycosidic bonds and triglycerides. Hydrolysis is the reverse process, using water to break large molecules into smaller components.
subtopic.why: These reactions underpin the formation and digestion of the major biological macromolecules — lipids, proteins and carbohydrates — and are essential for understanding both biochemistry and industrial organic chemistry.

items.title: I can write the equation for the hydrolysis of a protein or peptide to give amino acids
items.what: Peptide bonds in proteins are hydrolysed using water in the presence of enzymes (e.g. trypsin or pepsin in the digestive system) or aqueous HCl with heat. Each peptide bond broken consumes one water molecule and produces two amino acids (or smaller peptides).
items.why: Protein hydrolysis explains how dietary proteins are digested into amino acids that the body can use. It is also used analytically to determine the amino acid composition of a protein.
items.example: A tripeptide + 2H2O → 3 individual 2-amino acids (HCl, heat). Two peptide bonds are broken, consuming two water molecules.

subtopic.name: Condensation and Hydrolysis Reactions
subtopic.what: Condensation reactions join two molecules together with the release of a small molecule (usually water), forming esters, peptides, glycosidic bonds and triglycerides. Hydrolysis is the reverse process, using water to break large molecules into smaller components.
subtopic.why: These reactions underpin the formation and digestion of the major biological macromolecules — lipids, proteins and carbohydrates — and are essential for understanding both biochemistry and industrial organic chemistry.

items.title: I can write the equation for the condensation of alpha-glucose to form a disaccharide or polysaccharide with a glycosidic bond
items.what: Two alpha-glucose molecules react in a condensation reaction to form a disaccharide and water. The new C−O−C linkage between the two glucose units is called a glycosidic bond. Many glucose units condensing gives polysaccharides such as starch (amylose) and glycogen.
items.why: Starch and glycogen are the primary forms of carbohydrate energy storage in plants and animals respectively. Understanding their synthesis and the type of glycosidic bonds present (alpha-1,4 and alpha-1,6) is required by the Study Design.
items.example: Two alpha-glucose molecules → maltose (disaccharide) + H2O. The glycosidic bond forms between C1 of the first glucose and C4 of the second, making an alpha-1,4-glycosidic bond.

subtopic.name: Condensation and Hydrolysis Reactions
subtopic.what: Condensation reactions join two molecules together with the release of a small molecule (usually water), forming esters, peptides, glycosidic bonds and triglycerides. Hydrolysis is the reverse process, using water to break large molecules into smaller components.
subtopic.why: These reactions underpin the formation and digestion of the major biological macromolecules — lipids, proteins and carbohydrates — and are essential for understanding both biochemistry and industrial organic chemistry.

items.title: I can write the equation for the hydrolysis of starch or glycogen to give glucose
items.what: The glycosidic bonds in starch (amylose) and glycogen are broken by hydrolysis using water in the presence of enzymes. Each glycosidic bond hydrolysed consumes one water molecule and releases one glucose unit.
items.why: This reaction describes how stored carbohydrates are broken down to release glucose for cellular respiration. The branched structure of glycogen allows faster hydrolysis than linear amylose because it has more terminal glucose units.
items.example: Amylose (n glucose units) + (n−1)H2O → n alpha-glucose molecules (enzyme catalyst).

subtopic.name: Condensation and Hydrolysis Reactions
subtopic.what: Condensation reactions join two molecules together with the release of a small molecule (usually water), forming esters, peptides, glycosidic bonds and triglycerides. Hydrolysis is the reverse process, using water to break large molecules into smaller components.
subtopic.why: These reactions underpin the formation and digestion of the major biological macromolecules — lipids, proteins and carbohydrates — and are essential for understanding both biochemistry and industrial organic chemistry.

items.title: I can classify a transesterification reaction given an equation or description
items.what: Transesterification involves an ester reacting with an alcohol to form a new ester, with the original alcohol being released. The alcohol used in the reaction becomes the new alkyl group of the ester product.
items.why: Transesterification is listed separately from condensation and hydrolysis in the Study Design. Students must be able to distinguish it from esterification (which starts with a carboxylic acid) and from hydrolysis (which uses water, not an alcohol).
items.example: A triglyceride reacting with methanol (CH3OH) in the presence of NaOH gives fatty acid methyl esters and glycerol. Methanol becomes the new alkyl group of each ester product.

subtopic.name: Transesterification and Biodiesel
subtopic.what: Transesterification is a reaction between an ester and an alcohol, in the presence of a base catalyst, to form a new ester. When plant or animal triglycerides react with methanol or ethanol, the products are fatty acid methyl or ethyl esters, collectively known as biodiesel, along with glycerol.
subtopic.why: Biodiesel is a renewable alternative to fossil fuel-based petrodiesel. Understanding transesterification connects organic reaction chemistry to real-world sustainability and green chemistry contexts.

items.title: I can write the equation for the transesterification of a plant triglyceride with methanol to produce biodiesel and glycerol
items.what: A triglyceride reacts with three molecules of methanol (or ethanol) in the presence of NaOH catalyst. The three ester bonds in the triglyceride are each replaced by a new methyl ester bond, releasing glycerol. The NaOH acts as a catalyst and is not consumed overall.
items.why: This specific reaction is required by the Study Design. Students need to show the correct reactants (triglyceride + 3 methanol), products (3 fatty acid methyl esters + glycerol) and the NaOH catalyst.
items.example: Triglyceride + 3CH3OH → 3 fatty acid methyl esters (biodiesel) + C3H8O3 (glycerol), with NaOH as catalyst.

subtopic.name: Transesterification and Biodiesel
subtopic.what: Transesterification is a reaction between an ester and an alcohol, in the presence of a base catalyst, to form a new ester. When plant or animal triglycerides react with methanol or ethanol, the products are fatty acid methyl or ethyl esters, collectively known as biodiesel, along with glycerol.
subtopic.why: Biodiesel is a renewable alternative to fossil fuel-based petrodiesel. Understanding transesterification connects organic reaction chemistry to real-world sustainability and green chemistry contexts.

items.title: I can explain why biodiesel is considered a more sustainable fuel than petrodiesel
items.what: Biodiesel is produced from plant or animal triglycerides, which are renewable feedstocks that can be regrown. Petrodiesel is derived from crude oil, a finite non-renewable resource. Biodiesel also produces fewer net carbon dioxide emissions because the carbon it releases was recently absorbed from the atmosphere by the plant.
items.why: This connects transesterification chemistry to the green chemistry and sustainability principles in 9C. Exam questions often ask students to compare the environmental credentials of biodiesel and petrodiesel.
items.example: Canola oil (a renewable plant triglyceride) can be transesterified with methanol to give canola biodiesel. Unlike petrodiesel, this fuel does not deplete finite fossil fuel reserves.

When plant or animal triglycerides react with methanol or ethanol, the products are fatty acid methyl or ethyl esters, collectively known as biodiesel, along with glycerol.
subtopic.why: Biodiesel is a renewable alternative to fossil fuel-based petrodiesel. Understanding transesterification connects organic reaction chemistry to real-world sustainability and green chemistry contexts.

items.title: I can calculate the percentage yield of a single-step reaction given the actual yield and the mass of a reactant
items.what: Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100. The theoretical yield is calculated from the stoichiometry of the balanced equation using the moles of the limiting reagent. The actual yield is the mass of product actually obtained after the reaction.
items.why: Percentage yield tells chemists how efficiently a reaction converts starting materials into the desired product. A low yield indicates significant waste or side reactions.
items.example: 45 g of ethanol (0.98 mol) is oxidised to ethanoic acid. Theoretical yield = 0.98 mol × 60 g/mol = 58.7 g. If 38 g is obtained, percentage yield = (38/58.7) × 100 = 65%.

Percentage atom economy measures what proportion of the reactant atoms end up in the desired product. Green chemistry principles guide the design of safer, more efficient and more sustainable chemical processes.
subtopic.why: These concepts are essential for evaluating whether a chemical process is efficient, cost-effective and environmentally responsible. They are heavily assessed in VCE Chemistry Unit 4 and link directly to real-world industrial and environmental contexts.

items.title: I can calculate the mass of product formed when the percentage yield and mass of starting material are known
items.what: First calculate the theoretical yield using stoichiometry, then multiply by the fractional percentage yield: actual yield = (percentage yield / 100) × theoretical yield.
items.why: This calculation is used in industrial settings to predict how much product a process will deliver, which informs decisions about scale-up and cost.
items.example: But-2-ene + Br2 at 93% yield. 35 g of but-2-ene (0.625 mol) gives a theoretical yield of 135 g of product. Actual yield = 0.93 × 135 = 125 g.

items.title: I can calculate the overall percentage yield of a multi-step reaction pathway
items.what: The overall percentage yield of a multi-step pathway is found by multiplying the individual percentage yields of each step together. For example, for three steps with yields of 29%, 89% and 72%: overall yield = 0.29 × 0.89 × 0.72 × 100 = 19%.
items.why: Multi-step pathways accumulate yield losses at every step. Understanding this discourages unnecessarily long synthesis routes and motivates chemists to develop more efficient pathways.
items.example: A three-step synthesis of propanoic acid with step yields of 29%, 89% and 72% gives an overall yield of 0.29 × 0.89 × 0.72 × 100 = 19%.

items.title: I can calculate the percentage atom economy of a single-step reaction
items.what: Percentage atom economy = (molar mass of desired product / total molar mass of all products) × 100. Since mass is conserved, the denominator can also be written as the total molar mass of all reactants. Catalysts and solvents are not included.
items.why: Atom economy measures how wasteful a reaction is at the molecular level. A reaction with 100% atom economy (like a pure addition reaction) produces no by-products at all.
items.example: For CH3CH2CH2Cl + NH3 → CH3CH2CH2NH2 + HCl: M(desired product) = 59 g/mol, M(all products) = 59 + 36.5 = 95.5 g/mol. Atom economy = (59/95.5) × 100 = 61.8%.

items.title: I can calculate the percentage atom economy of a multi-step reaction pathway
items.what: For a multi-step pathway, the atom economy is calculated using all reactants added across every step (the starting organic material plus every reagent added in subsequent steps) in the denominator, and the molar mass of the final desired product in the numerator. The main organic compound is not double-counted.
items.why: Calculating pathway atom economy reveals the cumulative waste potential of a synthesis. Long pathways using stoichiometric reagents tend to have very low atom economy.
items.example: Pathway: ethane + Br2 (UV) → bromoethane + NH3 → ethanamine. Reactants: M(C2H6) + M(Br2) + M(NH3) = 30 + 159.8 + 17 = 206.8 g/mol. Atom economy = (45/206.8) × 100 = 21.8%.

items.title: I can discuss the advantages for society and industry of developing chemical processes with a high percentage atom economy
items.what: High atom economy means fewer by-products are formed. This reduces waste disposal costs and environmental impact, improves product purity (fewer by-products to separate), reduces hazard exposure for workers, and lowers the overall cost of production.
items.why: Exam questions frequently ask students to go beyond simply stating that fewer by-products are produced and to explain the downstream consequences for environment, safety, cost and product quality.
items.example: A reaction with 95% atom economy produces far less waste than one with 40% atom economy. This means the 95% process requires less waste treatment infrastructure, is cheaper to run and poses lower risks to workers handling the materials.

items.title: I can explain how the use of renewable feedstocks contributes to sustainable chemical production
items.what: Renewable feedstocks are raw materials that can be replenished faster than they are consumed, such as plant biomass, animal fats or waste materials. Using them reduces dependence on finite fossil fuel resources and can reduce waste by utilising by-products of other industries.
items.why: Renewable feedstocks are one of the three green chemistry principles specifically identified in the Study Design. Students need to apply this principle to specific examples such as bioethanol from sugar cane or biodiesel from plant oils.
items.example: Sugar cane is a renewable feedstock that can be harvested within one year. Glucose from sugar cane is fermented to produce bioethanol (C2H5OH), a versatile industrial solvent and fuel, without depleting fossil fuels.

items.title: I can explain how catalysis contributes to sustainable chemical production
items.what: Catalysts increase reaction rate without being consumed. This allows reactions to proceed under milder conditions (lower temperature and pressure), reduces energy consumption, decreases the time needed to obtain products and can reduce by-product formation compared to stoichiometric reagent-based alternatives.
items.why: Catalysis is one of the three green chemistry principles in the Study Design. The development of better catalysts can enable entirely new, more efficient reaction pathways, as demonstrated by the Hoechst ibuprofen synthesis.
items.example: The Hoechst Company process for ibuprofen uses two catalytic steps to complete the synthesis in three steps, compared to the original six-step stoichiometric process by Boots. This reduces waste, lowers cost and improves atom economy.

items.title: I can explain how designing safer chemicals contributes to sustainable chemical production
items.what: Designing safer chemicals means choosing starting materials, reagents and processes that have lower toxicity to humans and animals and a lower environmental impact. This includes replacing hazardous substances with structurally similar, less toxic alternatives where possible.
items.why: This is the third green chemistry principle in the Study Design. Students need to understand that sustainability is not only about energy and waste but also about the health and safety of workers, communities and ecosystems.
items.example: Toluene can replace benzene as a solvent in many organic reactions. Unlike benzene, which is oxidised in the liver to a carcinogen linked to leukaemia, toluene is oxidised to benzoic acid, a non-toxic compound.
